messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just after parent-teacher conferences. Marcus had been walking back to his car in the school parking lot, a stack of graded essays tucked under his arm, when a man stepped out from between two vans. There was no warning, no words exchanged—just a hand shoving him hard into the side of a minivan, the cold pressure of a blade against his ribs, and the command to hand over his wallet. Marcus complied instantly, but the man, smelling of sweat and stale cigarettes, leaned in close and whispered something about knowing where he worked. Then he was gone, taking Marcus’s wallet, his phone, and the quiet assumption that the world was basically safe.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found he could not shake the taste of bile and the metallic tang of fear that had flooded his mouth during those moments. That taste would rise unbidden in his throat when he least expected it—while grading papers in the empty classroom, or standing at the stove making dinner. The memory would crash over him with full sensory force: the cold metal, the man’s breath on his neck, the weight of the shove. He had no control over when it came, and it came often. What frightened him most was the way the memory seemed to rewrite the present—his own living room could suddenly feel like the parking lot.

Marcus had always been a steady presence in the classroom, but now he found himself scanning the faces of students’ parents during morning drop-off, reading their expressions for something hostile. He felt a deep, grinding injustice about what had happened—the man had been caught three weeks later, but had been released on a technicality, and Marcus was certain the system had failed him completely. The world, he now believed, was a place where people could hurt you and nothing would be done. This belief made the memories worse; every time he recalled the mugging, the unfairness of it burned fresh, and that burn made the memory feel even more vivid and intrusive.

Crowded places became unbearable. The supermarket on a Saturday morning, the hallway between classes, the faculty meeting room packed with chairs—each one felt like a trap. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator to avoid being pressed against strangers. Driving with his wife to visit her parents became a special kind of torment; the confined space, the traffic, the sense of being unable to escape—he would grip the door handle and watch the faces of drivers in adjacent cars, certain one of them was planning something. Loud noises, like a car backfiring or a door slamming in the school corridor, would yank him back into the parking lot, his heart hammering, the taste flooding back.

This hypervigilance, in turn, reinforced his belief that the world was dangerous. Every face he studied, every exit he noted, every flinch at a sudden movement—it all seemed to prove that he was right to be afraid. Already running on threat, Marcus found that ordinary moments turned into triggers with startling ease — a parent lingering too long at the classroom door, the scrape of a chair behind him in a meeting — each one feeling like the beginning of something worse. He had come to believe that if he stopped watching, stopped scanning, he would be caught off guard again. So he watched constantly, and the watching made him feel the world was full of threats, and that feeling of threat made the memories more frequent, because he was always on alert for the moment they might return. Living at that pitch of alertness, Marcus had come to see every hostile glance or unfair outcome as further proof that the world was fundamentally rigged against him — that the injustice of his mugging was not an exception but a rule.

The job that had once given him purpose now felt like a minefield. Last week, a student dropped a textbook in the back of the classroom, and Marcus had spun around so violently that the class had fallen silent. His wife had started to ask why he flinched when she touched his shoulder from behind. He had stopped going to the gym, stopped meeting friends for coffee. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he could not bring himself to walk through the school’s front doors—he stood in the parking lot, tasting that bile again, and knew he could not keep living this way. He was afraid that if he did not find a way out, the world he had built would collapse entirely.
